title: Gideon and the Interior
premise: Noor Halloran has spent nine years writing postcards to the burned house on Vell Street, where his sister Ada lived and died in a fire he believes he could have prevented. When a radio station plays an unrecorded song Ada once sang only for him, Noor realizes someone else survived that night and remembers her—and that the house's lot is being sold at month's end, erasing the last physical anchor to his grief. As he traces the song's origin through a small-town music scene that never knew Ada by name, Noor must finally inventory what he owes the living: her old bandmate Wren, who loved her too, and himself. The novel ends at the house sale closing, where Noor reads a letter aloud on the empty lot—saying goodbye properly at last, and choosing, for the first time, to be seen.
about_author: Kestrel Nystrom is the pen name of a former estate appraiser who spent a decade cataloguing other people's belongings before turning to fiction. Their work explores grief as an act of translation, and they live near a lake that freezes late and thaws early.

chapters.title: The Inventory of Unsaid Things
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. We meet him mid-ritual: writing postcard number 312 to the burned house on Vell Street, filing it unsent in a shoebox alongside lists of everything he never told Ada. The house is scheduled for sale; a notice arrives. Emotional beat: quiet dread disguised as routine.

chapters.title: A Song That Was Never Recorded
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. Driving home from work, the radio plays a melody Noor knows intimately—one Ada composed and sang only for him, never performed publicly. He pulls over, shaking. The DJ credits a local songwriter named Wren Marsh. Emotional beat: the past breaching the present.

chapters.title: Vell Street, Before
chapters.summary: Flashback chapter, Ada's POV rendered through Noor's memory. The house alive: Ada teaching him harmonies in the kitchen, their pact that she'd record her songs 'when it mattered.' Hints of the argument the night of the fire. Emotional beat: warmth shadowed by foreknowledge.

chapters.title: Wren Marsh
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. He finds Wren playing a Tuesday residency at a bar called the Interior. She performs Ada's song as her own—or so it seems. Noor doesn't confront her; he listens until closing. Emotional beat: suspicion tangled with recognition.

chapters.title: What the Fire Report Said
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. He requests the fire investigation file and rereads the official account: electrical fault, no survivors inside. But a witness statement mentions a second person seen leaving. Noor realizes Wren may have been there that night. Emotional beat: hope curdling into accusation.

chapters.title: Postcards, Interrupted
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. We learn Wren's side: she was Ada's secret collaborator and lover, escaped the fire, and has carried the songs forward because stopping felt like a second death. She noticed the man at her show who looked like grief itself. Emotional beat: guilt worn as devotion.

chapters.title: The Shoebox
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. His sister-in-law Priya visits, pressures him to clear out his storage unit where Ada's belongings sit untouched since the funeral. He opens the box of postcards and cannot explain them aloud. Emotional beat: shame at how grief has calcified into secrecy.

chapters.title: Two Truths About the Same Night
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. He returns to the Interior and confronts Wren between sets. She reveals she was there the night of the fire—that Ada sent her out the back door and stayed behind to retrieve the notebook of songs. Noor's certainty about his own guilt cracks. Emotional beat: collision of two survivor stories.

chapters.title: The Argument
chapters.summary: Flashback, fuller version of the fire-night fight: Ada had decided to move away and record her album elsewhere; Noor, drowning in his own failures, told her she'd never finish anything. She left angry. He stayed. The fire started hours later. Emotional beat: devastating context for his self-blame.

chapters.title: Buyer's Agent
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. The sale timeline accelerates—a developer wants the lot, closing in three weeks. Noor petitions to delay, citing sentimental value, and is politely refused. He begins visiting the lot nightly. Emotional beat: urgency forcing grief into motion.

chapters.title: Duet
chapters.summary: Alternating Noor/Wren POV. Reluctantly, they begin meeting: she plays fragments, he supplies lyrics only Ada's brother would know. Together they reconstruct the unfinished song Ada was writing when she died. Emotional beat: guarded collaboration becoming intimacy.

chapters.title: Priya's Question
chapters.summary: Priya's POV. She finds one of Noor's unsent postcards and confronts him—not with anger but with fear that he's been alone in a way she failed to see. She tells him about her own miscarriage, the goodbye she never got to say. Emotional beat: grief recognizing grief.

chapters.title: The Notebook
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. Wren produces Ada's songbook, salvaged from the fire, water-stained. In the margins: notes addressed to both of them. Ada knew Noor would blame himself; she wrote 'it wasn't your fault, it was wiring' weeks before the fire. Noor can't absorb it yet. Emotional beat: absolution arriving too early to be believed.

chapters.title: Invisible Man
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. A crisis at work exposes how thoroughly Noor has made himself invisible—passed over, forgotten, friendless by design. His boss offers a transfer to another city. For the first time, staying or going is a real choice. Emotional beat: the cost of hiding tallied.

chapters.title: Rising Action: The Developer
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren learns the developer plans a demolition permit immediately upon closing. She proposes something reckless: a public performance of Ada's finished song on the lot before the sale closes, forcing the town to remember what stood there. Noor refuses—he doesn't do public. Emotional beat: conflict between protection and witness.

chapters.title: What Survival Costs
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. Noor finally reads the full witness statement: Ada pushed Wren out because Wren panicked, and Ada chose to go back. It wasn't sacrifice for the songs—it was love, plain and terrible. Noor breaks down alone in the storage unit among her things. Emotional beat: the truth beneath all his theories.

chapters.title: Saying It Out Loud, First Draft
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. He attempts to write the goodbye letter and fails repeatedly—every draft an inventory of blame. Wren reads one over his shoulder and says gently: 'You're still writing to her like she's listening. Write it like you're the one who needs to hear it.' Emotional beat: the turn.

chapters.title: The Night Before Closing
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Wren and Noor rehearse in the empty house shell—walls stripped to studs, Ada's scorch mark still visible on the stairwell beam. They decide Noor will read the letter aloud at the lot tomorrow, whether anyone comes or not. Emotional beat: trembling resolve.

chapters.title: Climax: The Lot on Vell Street
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. Closing morning. Wren plays; a small crowd gathers—Priya, neighbors, even the buyer's agent. Noor stands on the lot and reads the letter aloud: everything unsaid, including 'I'm sorry,' 'thank you,' and 'I'm letting you go.' He mails the final postcard—to himself, at his own address. Emotional beat: catharsis, witnessed.

chapters.title: Aftermath
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The house comes down. Wren decides to record the album under both their names—Ada Halloran and Wren Marsh. She asks Noor to write the liner notes. He says yes before he can hide. Emotional beat: grief converted into legacy.

chapters.title: The Last Postcard
chapters.summary: Noor's POV. Weeks later, Noor declines the transfer and unpacks the storage unit into his apartment—Ada's guitar on his wall, her notebook on his desk. He writes postcard number 313, but this time he sends it: to Wren, with a lyric suggestion. Emotional beat: belonging chosen.

chapters.title: Interior
chapters.summary: Noor's POV, coda. At the album's first public performance, the crowd sings the chorus back to the stage—the song that was never recorded, now everyone's. Noor stays afterward, visible, unhurried, and walks home the long way past Vell Street, where new foundations are being poured. Emotional beat: survival, at last, worth its price.
